entries.content: Patient presented with worry about work performance, occasional racing thoughts before deadlines. Mild generalized anxiety noted. Recommended breathing exercises and follow-up in 6 weeks. Patient declined medication at this time.

I've been in practice for 18 years and find that patients do better when we build on existing frameworks rather than constantly questioning prior assessments. When someone comes in with new stress symptoms, I look at what's already documented and work from there. Reopening diagnoses creates confusion and can undermine the therapeutic relationship we've built. My patients appreciate that I trust the clinical picture we've established together.

Anxiety disorders commonly present with sleep disturbance and periods of heightened arousal, particularly during stressful life phases. If the patient has a documented history of anxiety and is experiencing these symptoms, it often makes sense to intensify the current treatment approach—perhaps adding sleep hygiene protocols or adjusting coping strategies—rather than introducing diagnostic uncertainty that could delay practical interventions.

Patients who have integrated a diagnosis into their self-understanding often experience distress when that diagnosis is questioned. Research on therapeutic alliance suggests that validating a patient's existing framework and working within it tends to improve engagement and treatment adherence. When patients request to continue with established approaches, honoring that preference supports autonomy and maintains trust in the clinical relationship.

Had a difficult session yesterday. Patient was frustrated when I explained we needed to look more carefully at some new symptoms before moving forward with the treatment plan. Took an extra 20 minutes and they left seeming annoyed. Part of the job I suppose, but these conversations are never easy when someone just wants to get on with things.
